directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Jubilee was bred in North Carolina and ripens early to midseason, producing large, firm, sweet, light-blue berries on a vigorous, productive bush well suited to warmer Southern growing conditions where lower-chill varieties are needed. The good heat tolerance for a highbush type makes it a solid choice for extending highbush blueberry production into milder climates than many Northern-bred varieties can handle. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out the oldest canes each winter to maintain vigor, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.

Brigitta was bred in Australia and became internationally popular for its exceptionally firm, large, late-ripening berries with outstanding shelf life, holding quality in storage and transit better than most highbush varieties, a trait that has made it a favorite for both commercial growers and home gardeners wanting fruit that keeps well after picking. Ripening late in the season, it extends the harvest window when planted alongside earlier varieties, and the vigorous, upright bush is a reliable, heavy producer once established. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out old canes each winter, and plant with a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.

planting.note: Set out bare-root or potted bushes in early spring once soil is workable, into strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark; Spartan is more particular about soil drainage and pH than many highbush varieties and performs best with attentive site preparation.

Spartan was bred at Michigan State University and remains one of the most flavorful early-season highbush blueberries available, producing very large, firm, intensely sweet berries widely regarded by growers as among the best-tasting of any early blueberry variety. The tradeoff for that exceptional flavor is a genuine sensitivity to soil conditions — Spartan performs best in well-drained, properly acidic soil and can struggle in heavier or poorly prepared sites where more forgiving varieties would tolerate the conditions fine. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out old canes each winter, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.

Bluegold was bred at Michigan State University for a compact, dense, cold-hardy growth habit that fits well into smaller home garden beds and large containers where full-sized highbush varieties would quickly outgrow the space, while still producing a solid midseason crop of sweet, firm, light-blue berries. The naturally tidy shape needs less aggressive pruning to keep in bounds than many vigorous highbush cultivars, making it a practical choice for gardeners with limited room or those growing blueberries primarily as an ornamental edible landscape plant. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune lightly each winter, and plant with a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.

Draper was released by Michigan State University in the 2000s and quickly became popular for producing exceptionally firm, crack-resistant, light-blue berries that hold their quality remarkably well after picking, a trait originally valued for mechanical harvesting but equally useful for home gardeners who want berries that keep well in the refrigerator. Ripening early to midseason on a vigorous, upright, productive bush, Draper combines good flavor with the kind of fruit durability that makes picking and storing a whole harvest far more forgiving than with softer-fruited varieties. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out old canes each winter, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.
